newsitem.title: FRANCE: France denies changing nuclear doctrine.
newsitem.headline: France denies changing nuclear doctrine.

text.p: France denied any change in nuclear doctrine on Thursday after German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe fuelled uproar in Paris by saying the French had for the first time accepted the supremacy of NATO's U.S. nuclear deterrent.

Ruehe's comment on German television gave fresh ammunition to France's left-wing opposition, which argues the government has sacrificed national defence sovereignty to the United States and NATO in a joint defence document with Bonn.
Misgivings about NATO extended to members of the ruling coalition, with two former defence ministers expressing doubts about the centre-right government's policy.

Ruehe said on Wednesday: "It is worth noting that France for the first time has signed a document in which NATO's nuclear defence is seen as the decisive element and the British and French nuclear systems back this up."

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt contradicted Ruehe, saying the Joint Franco-German Security and Defence Concept merely repeated word-for-word a text adopted by a 1991 NATO summit in Rome, attended by the late Socialist French President Francois Mitterrand.

Both texts declared: "The supreme guarantee of the Allies' security is ensured by the strategic nuclear forces of the Alliance, in particular those of the United States. The independent nuclear forces of the United Kingdom and France, which fulfil a deterrent role of their own, contribute to the global deterrence and security of the allies."
Rummelhardt suggested it was Germany, rather than France, which was modifying its doctrine by agreeing to discuss with France a European nuclear deterrence strategy.

"Our doctrine hasn't changed. The only new element on nuclear policy is that for the first time, France and Germany declare themselves ready to hold a dialogue concerning the nuclear concept in the context of a European defence policy," Rummelhardt said.
"French nuclear forces are recognised by Germany as having a special role in the context of European defence," he said.
A defence ministry official said Ruehe had presented the issue in a way that did not correspond to the text, and France would take the matter up with him.
The French Communist party demanded a full parliamentary debate and a vote on the Franco-German text.

On the right, veteran Pierre Messmer, defence minister for late president Charles de Gaulle, said Paris "have moved very clumsily towards NATO without obtaining anything" in its plan to re-enter NATO's military command after a 30-year break.

He added it was likely "we will be in a weaker position than when General de Gaulle decided to pull out". He predicted that Paris would fail in its drive to persuade Washington to let a European officer take over NATO's southern command.
And former defence minister Francois Leotard cautioned the government against moving closer to NATO if it did not win concessions from Washington on reform of the Alliance.

Leotard, president of the UDF, junior partner in the centre-right ruling coalition, told RTL radio: "I don't want us to go further without obtaining guarantees from the Americans on a number of issues -- on (southern) command, on procedures and on how Europeans can exist as themselves inside NATO."
Extreme-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen denounced the text adopted by President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Nuremberg on December 9.

"This agreement is shocking, in its form because it reflects a secret policy of abandoning our sovereignty, contrary to our constitution, as well as in content, since it codifies our submission to the interests of the New World Order and its military arm -- NATO," Le Pen said in a statement.
